Rada Krishna Bigraha (Deity) and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
9. Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in both the Rules, submits that the plaintiff Deity has been successful in proving her case, title and possession in respect of the suit land and the alleged sole decree obtained by the defendant in their earlier title Suit No. 331 of 1966 along with the order in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 inasmuch as the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1 was not a party in those proceedings. The learned Advocate further submits that the alleged auction sale in favour of defendant No. 3 Sikandar Ali was also collusive and fraudulent and without covering any actual possession or title to him and the alleged sale is nothing but a mere paper transaction as per own admission of the alleged auction purchaser defendant No. 3 and his alleged subsequent transferee, the defendant No. 13 Mohammad Ali, whose deposition, on the other hand, will speak for itself to show that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction. The learned Advocate further submits that it is claimed by the defendant No. 1 that he is the adopted son of Kulok but there is no evidence on record in respect of ceremony of giving and taking him as adopted son and the defendant-petitioner has miserably failed to prove his adoption. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that there is no document to show that the suit property is a Dabottar property but Ext. 2 series, the CS records and Ext. 1 series, the name BAND. go to show that the suit property was recorded successively in the names of Baishnabs as disciple of Guru and there is no description of the father's name of the Baishnabs which consequently prove that the suit property belonged to the Deity for more than 100 years and these documents, that is, the CS Khatian and the Jama Bandi are the admitted documents and their genuineness arc not disputed by the defendant-petitioner. From Ext. 1 CS Khatian No. 251 it is found that Kulak Das Boishnab has been described as disciple of Joyram Boishnab and there is a homestead and from the materials coupled with the oral testimony of PWs conclusively established that the suit properties are not secular or personal properties of Kulak Das or of the defendant No. 1 but are dedicated properties and owned by the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1. The learned Advocate further submits that besides Exts. 1 and 2 Ties there are sufficient oral evidence on record to show that the suit property is debottor property inasmuch as PWs 4, 5 and 11 have categorically stated that from time immemorial the property is being used for the Sheba Puja of the Deity and the Puja offered by the Shebayets, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been able to prove by sufficient oral evidence that the suit property is being used for the Deity for a long period of over 100 years and the legal position is that if the property is used for a period of 50 years or more for performing Sheba Puja to a Deity that becomes Debottar property and in the instant case the oral evidence of the PWs coupled with the Ext. 1 and 2 series established it beyond any doubt that by long user for over long 50 years the suit property has become Debottor property and in that view of the matter, the trial Court rightly relied on the decision reported in 11 DLR 372,16 DLR (SC) 457; 24 DLR (SC) 36 and in addition to that the learned Advocate also refers to and relies on the decision reported in 36 DLR 47 and the case reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 797. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that the defendant No. 1 petitioner has been residing in portion of the outer house to the south of the Deity house as servant of the Shebayet and Mon Mohan Das was installed as Sebayet of the Deity and has been in possession of the entire suit land on behalf of the Deity and, as such, the defendant No. 1 has been in possession of a part of the ditch land, that is, the portion of the house he has been living in just as a servant and he had every right over the same. The learned Advocate next submits that there are overwhelming evidence on record to show that the alleged Solenama obtained in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and the Solenama executed in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were obtained by the defendant petitioner through coercion, threat, intimidation by filing series of cases against Mon Mohan Das one after another both Civil and Criminal. The learned Advocate further submits that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation and undue influence is clear from the fact that immediately thereafter the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Das instituted the instant suit for declaration of title of the Deity to the suit property and for further declaration that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence and not binding upon the plaintiff. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant suit both the courts concurrently found that the suit is not hit by article 142 or 144 and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has instituted the same well within the period of limitation and both the courts below on proper appreciation of materials on record arrived at a finding to that effect and question of limitation is a question of fact and since the concurrent finding of both the courts below is based on materials and evidence on record there is no scope for this court to interfere with that finding of fact which by no stretch of imagination is perverse. The learned Advocate repels the submission of Dr Rafiqur Rahman that there is no evidence on record to show that the second schedule property was purchased by Kulak Das with the income of the Deity's property inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 himself as PW 1 categorically admitted in his cross-examination that Kulak purchased the second schedule property from the income of the property which he got from Saran Das Boishnab his Guru, and the name of this Saran Das Boishnab also appears in the record of right as Boishnab as disciple of his Guru. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the admission of DW 1 himself that the second schedule property was purchased with the income of the property of Saran Das and the absence of any documentary evidence from the side of the plaintiff Deity that the second scheduled property was purchased by Mulak Das as Shebayet of the Deity is not fatal and this will have no material bearing on the title of the Deity in respect of the second schedule property as the defendant No. 1 has admitted that the property was purchased with the income of the first schedule property. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that no issue has been framed on the alleged auction purchase of the third schedule land but this story of auction purchase of the third schedule land was not in the original written statement which had earlier been filed by the defendant Nos. 1-3 jointly and it is only when the suit came back to the trial Court on remand the defendant No. 3 for the first time introduced the story of auction purchase and sale to defendant No. 13 who is opposite party No. 26 in Civil Revision No. 3228 of 1992 and petitioner in the next revision, namely, Civil Revision No. 3229 of 1992. The parties led evidence on the point and the courts below taking into consideration the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, have concurrently found that the auction sale is nothing but a sham transaction and the original defendant No. 3 did never get possession of third schedule land through court in execution proceeding arising out of the money suit and the appellate Court below taking into consideration the evidence of defendant No. 3 himself arrived at a positive finding that the alleged auction sale is nothing but a paper transaction and the defendant No. 2 did not acquire any right, title and interest in respect of the third schedule land and the alleged sale made by him to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 on 3-4-67 did not create any right, title and interest in their favour. The learned Advocate next submits that both the courts below rightly found that the suit is not barred by limitation inasmuch as mainly it is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and admittedly Kulak died on 25-12-1372. BS that is, some time in early part of 1965 and thereafter, the defendant No. 1 claiming himself as adopted son of Kulak filed a suit for permanent injunction, that is Title Suit No. 331 of 1966, and that suit was filed on 7-9-66 and it is alleged by the plaintiff Deity that the sole decree in suit No. 331 of 1966 has been obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation and undue influence and, as such, the Deity filed the present suit on 4-12-67 for declaration of its title and recovery of possession as well as for declaration that the sole decrees are null and void and obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation, and not binding upon the Deity and, as such, the suit was filed within two years from the date of death of Kulak. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant No.13 purchased the suit land on 3-4-67 and the defendant No. 13 also purchased some portion of the suit land from third schedule land from Sikandar on 3-4-67 and some other portions of the third schedule land from defendant No. 14 on 31-3-80 and the suit was filed well within 12 years from the date of this transaction and, in that view of the matter, the courts below did not commit any illegality and concurrently found that the suit is not barred by limitation under article 142 or 144 of the Limitation Act. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that none of the courts below considered Exhibit 0 but on a perusal of Ext. ''O'' it appears that this document, in fact, supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. In Ext. ''O'' it is stated that the defendant No.1 resides in the outer house which is situated within the suit land and it is also seen from Ext. ''O'' that there is a temple there though it has not been specifically mentioned that there is a Deity in the temple, but fact remains that a temple cannot be without any Deity and this shows that there was a Deity in the temple and on top of that there are oral evidences of the PWs to show that there is a Deity in the temple and Seba Puja is performed during Rath Jatra. Rash Jatra and Jhulan Jatra by the devotees and Shebayets of the Deity. The learned Advocate emphatically submits that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in the instant suit has paid ad-valorem court fees and prays for recovery of possession of the entire suit land and it is only after review of the evidence by the courts below they have found that the plaintiff Deity is not ousted from the entire suit land and is still in possession of the major portion of the suit land and, as such, decreed the suit declaring title of the Deity to the suit land, followed by confirmation of possession in respect of the land which are in possession of the Deity and decree for delivery of khas possession for that portion of the suit land where the defendant No. 1 is found to be in possession. Since the plaintiff has paid ad-valorem court fees on the entire suit land and since the plaintiff Deity has been successful in establishing her title to the suit land, it is immaterial in which portion or to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and since the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land, it is immaterial to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and the suit cannot be dismissed for not specifying the exact areas which is in possession of the defendant petitioner. The learned Advocate further submits that the omission to specify the exact area which is in occupation of the defendant petitioner is not fatal in the instant case, inasmuch as title of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been found in favour of the Deity and the suit is filed within the period of limitation. The learned Advocate next submits that the courts below did not commit any illegality in passing a decree for khas possession after evicting the defendant petitioner from the portion of the suit land which is found in his possession because under Order 7 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure a court is empowered to grant any relief to a party if it is found on consideration of the materials and evidence on record that the plaintiff has been able to establish his case to that effect and in support of his submission he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1963 (Punjab) 538, AIR 1942 (Pat) 247; AIR 1952 (SC) 47; 16 DLR 510; 14 DLR 307; AIR 1970(M) 40; AIR 1957 (All) 784. The learned Advocate finally submits that even if there be some lacuna in the impugned judgment this court sitting under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is competent to go through the records and the evidence adduced by the parties and on appraisal of the same if the court is of opinion that there are sufficient materials and evidence on record to ultimately sustain the impugned judgment, this court will not interfere with the same. The learned Advocate further submits that in an appropriate case, this court is entitled to enter into the merits of the case and decide the same finally, when the entire records are before it and this is the consistent view of our Appellate Division as has been taken in decisions, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 31; 43 DLR (AD) 78, 82, 125, and 44 DLR (AD) 98. The learned Advocate finally submits that on a perusal of the evidence and material on record, it is crystal clear that there are sufficient evidence and materials on record to show that the suit property actually belonged to the Deity opposite party No. 1 and the successive Boishnabs were managing the property as Shebayet of the Deity and applied the income of the suit property in performing Seba Puja of the Deity and therefore, the courts below did not commit any illegality in finding title of the Deity to the suit property and also in finding that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and that the suit is filed within time and the materials and evidence on record clearly supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. As such, there has been no error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice calling for any interference by this court. 

 13. The second plank of attack made by Dr Rahman is that the prayer is vague and unspecific. The plaintiff Deity did not specifically state in her plaint as to when and from what portion of the suit land she was dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 and, as such, the decree passed by the courts below is not sustainable in law. It appears that the instant suit is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the plaintiff has paid ad valorem court-fees on the entire suit land, and initially prayed for recovery of possession of the entire suit land after evicting the defendant No. 1 from the suit land. Both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land except certain portion where the defendant No. 1 lives in the homestead plot and, as such, decreed the suit is favour of the plaintiff and passed a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defendant No. 1 from that portion of the suit land where he is found in possession. The case of the defendant No.1 is that he is in possession of the entire suit land, where as the case of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is that he is in permissive occupation of the suit land and he has no right, title and interest in the suit land and the defendant No.1 admittedly was brought to the suit land by Kulak. The further case of the plaintiff is that he was brought to the suit land by Kulak, the then Shebayet of the Deity and he used to perform the domestic work. The dispute arose between the parties only after the death of Kulak, when the defendant No. 1 claimed himself as the adopted son of Kulak and claimed the suit property as personal property of Kulak and he filed Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and thereafter, the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Boishnab filed the instant suit in 1967. It is also admitted fact that Kulak Das died on 25th Chaitra, 1372, BS. It thus appears that the plaintiffs brought suit within 2 years from the date of death of Kulak and when the plaintiff No. 1 raised his claim to the suit property as his own property as heir of Kulak. It has already been noted that the appellate Court below on due consideration of the material and evidence on record found that the auction purchase is a sham transaction and that did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the defendant No. 3 in respect of land of schedule 3. Besides defendant No. 3 sold the suit land in 1967 to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 and defendant No. 13 purchased some portion of the third schedule land from defendant No.14 in 1980. It is, thus crystal clear that the finding of the appellate Court below that the suit is not barred by limitation is borne out by sufficient materials and evidence on record. Since the suit is a suit for declaration of title followed by recovery of possession both the courts below, in my opinion, did not commit any illegality by passing a decree declaring title of the Deity to the suit land followed by claim of possession in the suit land and also by passing a decree for khas possession of that portion of land which is found to be in occupation of the defendant No. 1. Since the plaintiff Deity has paid ad-valorem court fees for the entire suit land, if her title is established in the suit land she is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land and since she is already in possession of major portion of the suit land, she is entitled to get recovery of possession of that portion of land which is in possession of defendant. In that view of the matter I do not find any substance in this submission of Dr Rahman.
